title: Margins of a New Ledger
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 41 · Lanternweald continuation
content:
Severus Snape had agreed to volunteer at Moonroot Archive on the understanding that nobody would describe him as a volunteer.

The arrangement lasted precisely six days.

On the seventh, someone pinned a notice to the archive door.

VOLUNTEER CONSULTATION HOURS — SEVERUS SNAPE.

I found him staring at it.

His expression was a carefully composed argument for arson.

“Good morning,” I said.

“Is it?”

“Depends whether you're planning to set the building on fire.”

“I was considering something less dramatic.”

“What?”

“Removing the notice.”

“An act of great restraint.”

He detached the paper from its pin with the sort of precision normally reserved for extracting a venomous fang. Then he read it again, lips thinning at the word *volunteer*.

“I offered two hours of technical consultation,” he said. “By appointment. On alternate Thursdays.”

“Which is not the same as every Thursday.”

“Nor, I might add, is it the same as answering questions from anyone who wanders inside clutching a bottle.”

“Some bottles are very interesting.”

“Most bottles are mislabeled.”

He folded the notice once and handed it to me.

“Find the person responsible.”

I raised an eyebrow.

“Ask,” he corrected, after a moment. “Please ask the person responsible to amend it.”

I smiled.

He looked annoyed that I had noticed.

The archive smelled of paper, polished wood, and the damp earth beneath its roots. A narrow line of moisture had appeared on the west wall overnight despite the dry weather in the square. Several labels on the material shelves had curled at the corners.

Neri was at the central desk, sorting maintenance requests into three piles. The piles were headed URGENT, POSSIBLE, and SOMEBODY'S PROBLEM. I did not think the third category was official.

“We have a notice problem,” I said.

Neri looked at Severus, then at the folded page in my hand.

“Oh. That.”

“An illuminating explanation,” he said.

“I copied the schedule from the public ledger. Sorry.”

“Then the ledger is wrong.”

Neri opened the book.

The schedule recorded a full day of archive visits, with Severus's name in dark ink across the top. Beside it stood a second entry, written much smaller, listing the two alternate Thursday hours he had actually agreed to.

“That's strange,” Neri said. “I copied the shorter one.”

The longer entry bore a faded stamp: THRESHOLD CREW.

Severus put two fingers beside the stamp.

“Who authorized this?”

“I'm not sure.”

“Then nobody should have published it.”

Neri's shoulders dropped. “You're right. I'll correct the notice.”

He looked ready to continue. I could see the old instinct gathering, the desire to defend a boundary by making sure nobody ever considered crossing it again.

Then he stopped.

“Thank you,” he said.

Neri looked as surprised as I felt.

The notice came down. A revised one went up twenty minutes later, in the sharpest handwriting I had ever seen.

CONSULTATION BY APPOINTMENT. ALTERNATE THURSDAYS. NO UNLABELED MATERIALS. NO EXCEPTIONS WITHOUT PRIOR AGREEMENT.

It was not welcoming.

It was accurate.

We began our work in the small warded room off the archive hall. A crate from the Jasmine Steps had arrived with a damp paper seal and a packet of herbs inside. The label claimed they were appropriate for soothing burns. Severus disagreed before he opened it.

“You can tell from the smell?” I asked.

“From the description.”

“I haven't read you the description.”

“You are holding the packet upside down. The written dosage is visible through the paper.”

I turned it over.

He looked insufferably pleased.

The herbs themselves were harmless in the amounts intended for tea. A note beside them suggested a concentrated preparation for treating skin irritation.

“That would be unwise,” he said.

“Because?”

“Because a concentration intended for consumption is not automatically suitable for broken skin.”

I wrote it down.

He watched.

“You have missed a qualification.”

“Of course I have.”

“Which part is intended for consumption?”

I looked again and added the exact name of the blend.

“Happy?”

“Not yet.”

I smiled. “A lifelong condition.”

We worked through the packet with gloves and careful instruments. He had insisted on the gloves. I had insisted on a dry table. Neither requirement was especially romantic, which may have been why the morning felt unexpectedly peaceful.

Then I found the second label.

It was stuck to the underside of the crate, almost dissolved from the damp. The ink had blurred, but I could make out the same stamp that appeared in the ledger.

THRESHOLD CREW.

The same hand had recorded two different destinations.

Moonroot Archive.

Community kitchen.

The shipment could not have been delivered to both.

I held up the paper.

“Severus.”

He glanced at it once.

“Ah.”

“Ah?”

“A discrepancy.”

“Your favorite kind of thing.”

“Hardly. A discrepancy implies somebody will soon demand that I fix it.”

We carried both labels to the front desk. Neri compared the writing, then reached for the larger maintenance ledger.

“Can we check who signed them?” they asked.

“Only if they agreed to be entered,” I said.

Neri paused.

It was a small point, but not a trivial one. After the Threadrain began, people had suggested posting every visitor's name beside the doors. The reason was safety. The consequence would be a public record of everyone's movements, including people who had good reasons to keep their private lives private.

Severus examined the ledger.

“A record of deliveries is necessary,” he said. “A record of personal relationships is not. The two should not be confused merely because both are difficult to manage.”

Neri looked relieved.

“Exactly,” I said.

He glanced at me.

“Do not look so astonished. Privacy is not an exotic theory.”

“No. Just one you've applied with admirable efficiency.”

“I would prefer you describe it as basic competence.”

“Very well. You're basically competent.”

He gave me a withering look. It failed because I was already laughing.

We eventually found the cause of the duplicate shipment entry. During a night of Threadrain, the same crate had been moved from the kitchen to the archive so its contents could be inspected. Someone had logged the transfer as a new delivery. Someone else had copied that line into the wrong column.

Nothing had been stolen.

But the error had started a rumor that several people had already repeated as fact.

Neri erased the duplicate, then stopped with the chalk hovering over the board.

“Should we say who made the mistake?”

Severus considered the question.

“Is that necessary to prevent it happening again?”

“No.”

“Then describe the faulty procedure, not the person.”

I looked at him.

He pretended not to notice.

In the afternoon, we walked back toward the Moonroot Door carrying the corrected ledger. A few drops of Threadrain struck the stone path, cold and unexpected.

At the threshold, Severus stopped.

“You have somewhere else to be this evening,” he said.

“Yes. We discussed it yesterday.”

“We did.”

“Are you asking me to change the plan?”

“No.” He tightened his grip on the ledger. “I am informing you that our discussion was adequate. I would prefer we continue to be specific.”

The words were dry. The choice behind them was not.

I touched his sleeve.

“Thank you.”

He looked down at my hand.

“Was that approval?”

“Possibly.”

“An intolerable habit.”

“Yours or mine?”

He drew me closer, with enough time for me to step away. I did not. His kiss was brief in the open air, but the warmth of it stayed after he drew back.

“You will make me sentimental,” he said.

“You're already making a schedule.”

“A grave accusation.”

I laughed, and he went through the doorway toward Spinner's End while I stayed behind to help Neri put the ledgers away.

That night, I looked again at the damaged page. The duplicate entry made sense now.

The other mismatched records did not.

Three requests carried the same stamped time and different locations. Each had been written during a dry hour beneath a dripping lamp.

The error was larger than one crate.

It was not, I thought, larger than a group of people willing to ask exactly what had happened before deciding whom to blame.
